{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_ilwnaye7ka37b53ybalozcceufxpqkope4k62davmpwmu6wleaeq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Zero-downtime cloud migration of the on-prem patient scheduling system\n\n**Assumptions** (each one changes the plan if it's wrong):\n- **(a)** The scheduling app is self-hosted, either built in-house or a vendor product you run yourselves. If the vendor offers a hosted/SaaS version, see the Build-vs-buy gate.\n- **(b)** It's a single relational database behind an app tier, linked to the EHR through an interface engine (Mirth, Rhapsody or Cloverleaf) using HL7 v2 messages: SIU for scheduling, ADT for admissions and patient updates.\n- **(c)** The target cloud is one you already have a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with.\n- **(d)** The users are schedulers, the call center, clinics and the patient portal.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** Moving a live, clinically critical scheduling system (database, app, integrations) from on-prem to the cloud while it keeps serving users.\n- **Type:** Mostly infra, with some software work (a routing layer in front of the app, cutover controls, reconciliation tooling).\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Correctness, plus compliance.** Bookings must stay exactly right and patient data (PHI) must stay inside HIPAA controls. Availability comes second, and it can't be traded against correctness.\n- **Worst failure:** **The two copies of the data quietly drift apart.** An appointment is lost or double-booked, or the EHR gets the wrong SIU message. A patient misses care and nothing alerts anyone. That's worse than a visible outage, because hospitals have downtime procedures for outages but nothing catches silent corruption.\n\n> **Definition of \"without downtime\" (needs clinical-operations sign-off before Phase 5):** reads (schedule views, availability lookups) never stop. Bookings pause for **≤ 2 minutes** once, at the lowest-volume hour, with users warned in the UI and the call center briefed. Truly zero write pause would mean both systems accepting writes at once, and for a booking system that risks double-booking. That's the worst failure above, so this plan doesn't do it unless the flip condition below is met.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **Consistency for writes.** Only one side (on-prem or cloud) accepts bookings at any moment. Authority moves in one controlled, logged step. Reads may come from a replica only while replication lag is under the threshold. | None for writes. If a network split between sites makes the system unavailable longer than downtime procedures can cover, use read-only mode plus paper downtime procedures. Never let both sides accept writes. |\n| **Who accepts writes during migration** | **Single writer, moved in a ≤ 2-minute freeze** | Leadership requires literally zero write pause. Then build a write proxy that queues bookings and checks idempotency, which costs about 6–10 more weeks and needs its own rehearsals. |\n| **Migration depth** | **Replatform:** same app build, same database engine, on a managed database (e.g., RDS / Azure SQL MI). Users see no UI change and need no retraining. | Database licensing on the cloud is too expensive or the engine is unsupported. Then change engines as a **separate later project**, never in the same cutover. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Keep the monolith.** The only new piece is a thin routing layer (a reverse proxy plus DNS names) in front of it. | One function (e.g., reminders, or portal availability lookups) needs to scale independently. Split it out after Phase 6. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Async change-data-capture (CDC) replication** for data (AWS DMS / Debezium / GoldenGate, matched to the engine). **Synchronous** writes to whichever side is the single writer. HL7 stays async through the interface engine. | Replication lag p99 > 5 s during the rehearsal window, or CDC can't capture some tables (no primary key, or LOB columns). Then fix the schema or snapshot those tables during the freeze. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy** managed infrastructure: managed database, managed CDC, managed load balancer and firewall, the cloud key service. **Build** only reconciliation, diff tooling and the cutover runbook. | The vendor offers a certified SaaS version. Then this becomes a vendor-led data migration, but gates 1–2 and Phases 1, 4 and 5 still apply. |\n| **Cloud / PHI boundary** | Your existing cloud with a signed BAA, HIPAA-eligible services only, one region inside the jurisdiction, keys you manage, **no public endpoints**. | The portal needs an internet-facing endpoint. Add a WAF-fronted public tier after a pen test (Phase 3). |\n| **Hybrid connectivity** | Dedicated circuit (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute) **plus a site-to-site VPN as failover**. Order it on day 1 because circuits take 6–12 weeks to provision. | The circuit isn't delivered in time. Run Phase 0–1 over a redundant VPN, but **no write cutover over VPN only**. |\n| **(AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune** | N/A | Not an AI system. |\n| **(AI) hosted API vs self-host** | N/A | Not an AI system. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**The one real request:** a scheduler opens *\"Today's appointments for Dr. X, Clinic Y.\"* The cloud stack serves it from replicated data, and the answer is checked against on-prem's answer for the same request.\n\n**Tiers it crosses:**\n1. Scheduler workstation → hospital DNS, using a new name you control, e.g., `sched.hosp.internal`, that points to a pass-through proxy.\n2. Proxy (NGINX/Envoy, on-prem, initially just forwarding) → hybrid link → private load balancer and WAF in the cloud.\n3. → The app container, the **same build hash as on-prem**, running in a read-only mode, on ECS/AKS.\n4. → Login via SSO federated to hospital AD/Entra, with MFA.\n5. → The managed database replica, fed by CDC from the on-prem database. Phase 0 replicates only the *appointment, slot, provider, location and patient-demographics-reference* tables.\n6. → The real response goes back to 3 pilot schedulers.\n\nAt the same time, the proxy **mirrors** all real read requests of this type to the cloud and compares the cloud's answer with on-prem's. Users always get the on-prem answer, so mirrored traffic has no user impact.\n\n**Deployed, logged, monitored on day 0:**\n- **Deployed:** all of it via Terraform and a CI pipeline (landing zone, network, database, app, proxy config).\n- **Logged:** OpenTelemetry traces cover proxy → app → database. Logs are structured and stripped of PHI, and go to the hospital SIEM. Who-viewed-which-patient access audit logs go to the same audit store as on-prem.\n- **Monitored:** dashboards and alerts for replication lag, cloud vs on-prem diff rate, p95 latency, error rate, and a once-a-minute synthetic check.\n\n**Exit check:** a pilot scheduler's real request gets a correct answer from the cloud in production, with a full trace, a lag metric, and a diff result visible on the dashboard. On-prem is untouched and still the only system accepting bookings.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n**Phase 0: Walking skeleton** (above)\n- Unlocks: proof that the hybrid link, identity, CDC, the app build and observability all work end-to-end.\n- Depends on: signed BAA, landing zone, connectivity (VPN acceptable here).\n- Tasks, widest first:\n  1. BAA and the PHI boundary.\n  2. Network and identity federation.\n  3. Pass-through proxy and the DNS name.\n  4. CDC for the core tables.\n  5. Read-only app deploy.\n  6. Request mirroring and diffing.\n  7. Dashboards.\n- Exit: as in §3.\n\n**Phase 1: Data substrate (complete, provable replication)**\n- Unlocks: everything after it. Nothing reads from or writes to the cloud database broadly until this is proven.\n- Depends on: Phase 0 CDC working on the core tables.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Dependency inventory.** Every database, file share, batch job, report, ODBC/thick client, hard-coded IP or hostname, and inbound/outbound interface. This is the widest blast radius, because a consumer you miss breaks at cutover.\n  2. Freeze the schema contract (DDL changes only through migrations-as-code during the program).\n  3. Extend CDC to the **full schema** and any other databases the inventory finds.\n  4. **Continuous reconciliation:** per-table row counts every hour, column checksums every night, and an appointment-level comparison of slots booked per provider per day.\n  5. Re-snapshot procedure, tested.\n  6. Repoint the thick clients and reports found in the inventory to DNS names you control. They still resolve to on-prem.\n- Exit: replication lag p99 < 5 s for **14 consecutive days**, zero unexplained reconciliation mismatches for 7 days, and every inventory item has an owner and a migration path.\n\n**Phase 2: Integration layer in shadow**\n- Unlocks: cloud-side HL7/FHIR traffic that can be switched over later.\n- Depends on: Phase 1. The cloud data must be trustworthy before you compare messages generated from it.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Stand up the interface-engine channels in the cloud from version-controlled exports.\n  2. **Inbound ADT/MPI (patient index) feeds copied** to the cloud. The cloud processes them, but the replicated data stays authoritative.\n  3. Cloud **generates outbound SIU in shadow** (not sent) and compares it field by field with on-prem's real SIU.\n  4. FHIR/portal API endpoints, read-only.\n  5. Reminder/SMS vendor connectivity tested with a test-only sender.\n- Exit: zero outbound SIU differences across all event types (S12–S15, S17, S26) for 7 days, and every interface partner has signed off on the connectivity test.\n\n**Phase 3: Read-path cutover (progressive, reversible)**\n- Unlocks: real load on the cloud, and proof that it performs as well as on-prem.\n- Depends on: Phases 1–2. Replicated data is proven, and shadow comparisons are clean.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Lag-gated routing in the proxy: serve reads from the cloud only while replication lag is under 5 s, otherwise fall back to on-prem automatically.\n  2. Canary rollout: 5% → 25% → 100% of read traffic, one department at a time, with the emergency department and surgery scheduling last.\n  3. Patient-portal availability lookups (pen test first if it's public).\n  4. Reports and analytics moved to the cloud replica.\n- Exit: 100% of reads served from the cloud for 14 days, p95 latency at or below the on-prem baseline, no stale-read incidents, and automatic fallback exercised at least once in production.\n\n**Phase 4: Rollback path and rehearsals (must be proven before any write moves)**\n- Unlocks: the write cutover, because now it can be undone without losing data.\n- Depends on: Phase 3 proving the cloud can carry production load.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Reverse CDC (cloud → on-prem)**, built and validated in a production-like environment.\n  2. Point-in-time restore of the cloud database, actually performed and timed.\n  3. Cutover runbook as scripts, with go/no-go criteria and rollback triggers.\n  4. **3 full dress rehearsals** on a production-sized copy: freeze → drain → verify → switch authority → reverse CDC → **rollback**.\n  5. Game days: kill an availability zone, cut the dedicated circuit, kill the CDC task.\n  6. Clinical-operations sign-off on the ≤ 2-minute freeze, the cutover date, and the downtime-procedure standby.\n- Exit: 3 rehearsals in a row finish within time (freeze ≤ 2 min, rollback ≤ 15 min, zero data loss confirmed by reconciliation), the dedicated circuit is live, and the sign-off is recorded.\n\n**Phase 5: Write-authority cutover**\n- Unlocks: the cloud becomes the system of record.\n- Depends on: Phase 4 exit. A proven rollback path is required.\n- Tasks, in rehearsed order. This order is dictated by the procedure, not by blast radius.\n  1. Change freeze; no other changes allowed, including EHR upgrades or template edits.\n  2. Command center staffed (IT, clinical ops, interface team, vendor).\n  3. The app shows a \"read-only\" banner, and in-flight writes drain.\n  4. Confirm lag = 0 and checksums match.\n  5. Flip the authority flag, so the cloud accepts writes and on-prem becomes read-only.\n  6. Start reverse CDC.\n  7. Switch outbound SIU to the cloud engine and quiesce the on-prem engine.\n  8. Smoke-book a test patient, then release the banner.\n  9. Hypercare for 72 h.\n- Exit: write freeze ≤ 2 min; booking volume within ±10% of the same hour last week; zero interface NACKs (rejected messages) above baseline; reverse-CDC lag < 5 s; no rollback trigger hit in 72 h.\n\n**Phase 6: Stabilize, replace DR, decommission**\n- Unlocks: shutting down on-prem.\n- Depends on: Phase 5 stable for 30 days, **and** a replacement DR proven. On-prem is your DR until then.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Cross-region backup/restore DR with a target RPO ≤ 5 min and RTO ≤ 4 h, tested.\n  2. Run reverse CDC for 30 days, then retire it.\n  3. Archive on-prem data under records retention and legal hold.\n  4. Sanitize media (NIST 800-88) and collect certificates of destruction.\n  5. Remove proxy fallback routes.\n- Exit: a DR restore drill passes, on-prem is powered off with no consumers left (checked against the Phase 1 inventory), and the risk analysis is updated.\n\n## 5. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **0** | BAA; HIPAA-eligible services only; private endpoints; SSO + MFA; keys you manage; PHI-scrubbed logs; access-audit parity | OTel traces through every tier; lag, diff, latency and error metrics; synthetic check; SIEM feed | Terraform landing zone; app container built from the **same pinned commit** as on-prem; CI pipeline | On-prem stays the only writer; mirrored traffic has no user impact; redundant VPN tunnels |\n| **1** | Least-privilege read-only CDC account; TLS on replication; data classification; HIPAA risk analysis updated | Reconciliation dashboard (counts, checksums, slot comparison); lag alert as a service-level target | Schema migrations as code; CDC task config in git; baseline snapshot with recorded checksum | CDC resumes from checkpoint; re-snapshot procedure tested; multi-AZ database |\n| **2** | HL7 traffic wrapped in TLS/VPN; FHIR OAuth scopes (SMART on FHIR); interface credentials in a secrets manager | Per-channel message counts, ACK/NACK rates, queue depth; SIU comparison report | Interface channels exported to git; **replayable corpus of de-identified HL7 test messages** | Durable engine queues with replay; the on-prem engine stays primary |\n| **3** | WAF; pen test before any public portal traffic; access-audit continuity verified per department | Per-department targets; browser monitoring of real users; ongoing comparison sampling at 1% | Routing rules and canary percentages as audited feature flags in git | **Lag-gated automatic fallback** to on-prem; canary in steps with automatic halt on target breach |\n| **4** | Rehearsal environment holds production PHI, so it gets full production controls; break-glass accounts set up and tested | Every rehearsal step timed and recorded; rollback timing measured | Rehearsal environment built from the same IaC; runbook as scripts; repeat rehearsals must give consistent timings | Reverse CDC; point-in-time restore performed; game days (AZ loss, circuit loss, CDC loss) |\n| **5** | Privileged sessions recorded; just-in-time admin access; credentials rotated after cutover | Cutover dashboard: write success, booking rate vs baseline, NACKs, reverse-CDC lag | Run the rehearsed scripts exactly; tagged release; nothing improvised | Go/no-go gates; rollback triggers with a time limit; downtime procedures and paper schedules staffed |\n| **6** | On-prem credentials revoked; media sanitization certified; retention and legal hold kept | Steady-state targets and on-call routing; cost baseline | Full rebuild of the environment from IaC and backups in a scratch account | Cross-region DR proven **before** on-prem goes away; restore drill passes |\n\n## 6. AI layer\n**N/A.** This isn't an AI or agentic system. If AI features come later (e.g., no-show prediction, slot optimization), they're deferred below.\n\n## 7. Deliberately deferred\n- **Database engine change (e.g., Oracle → Postgres).** Do it when licensing cost justifies it, as its own project after Phase 6. Never in the same cutover.\n- **Splitting the monolith into services.** Do it when one function shows a scaling or release-speed bottleneck after Phase 6.\n- **Active-active multi-region.** Do it when an RTO under 1 h is required, or a regional outage causes a clinical incident. It also requires solving the single-writer problem.\n- **Truly zero write pause (queuing write proxy).** Build it if clinical leadership rejects the ≤ 2-minute freeze in Phase 4 sign-off.\n- **Replacing HL7 v2 with native FHIR integration.** Do it when the EHR vendor or partners require FHIR, or the interface engine reaches end of life.\n- **New features** (self-scheduling expansion, waitlist automation, AI no-show prediction): only after Phase 6. Migration and features must not change at the same time.\n- **Public portal tier.** Only if the portal must hit the cloud directly from the internet. If the vendor offers a hosted/SaaS version, see the Build-vs-buy gate.\n- **(b)** It's a single relational database behind an app tier, linked to the EHR through an interface engine (Mirth, Rhapsody or Cloverleaf) using HL7 v2 messages: SIU for scheduling, ADT for admissions and patient updates.\n- **(c)** The target cloud is one you already have a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with.\n- **(d)** The users are schedulers, the call center, clinics and the patient portal.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification\n- **What:** Moving a live, clinically critical scheduling system (database, app, integrations) from on-prem to the cloud while it keeps serving users.\n- **Type:** Mostly infra, with some software work (a routing layer in front of the app, cutover controls, reconciliation tooling).\n- **Dominant constraint:** **Correctness, plus compliance.** Bookings must stay exactly right and patient data (PHI) must stay inside HIPAA controls. Availability comes second, and it can't be traded against correctness.\n- **Worst failure:** **The two copies of the data quietly drift apart.** An appointment is lost or double-booked, or the EHR gets the wrong SIU message. A patient misses care and nothing alerts anyone. That's worse than a visible outage, because hospitals have downtime procedures for outages but nothing catches silent corruption.\n\n> **Definition of \"without downtime\" (needs clinical-operations sign-off before Phase 5):** reads (schedule views, availability lookups) never stop. Bookings pause for **≤ 2 minutes** once, at the lowest-volume hour, with users warned in the UI and the call center briefed. Truly zero write pause would mean both systems accepting writes at once, and for a booking system that risks double-booking. That's the worst failure above, so this plan doesn't do it unless the flip condition below is met.\n\n## 2. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Default (chosen now) | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Consistency vs availability** | **Consistency for writes.** Only one side (on-prem or cloud) accepts bookings at any moment. Authority moves in one controlled, logged step. Reads may come from a replica only while replication lag is under the threshold. | None for writes. If a network split between sites makes the system unavailable longer than downtime procedures can cover, use read-only mode plus paper downtime procedures. Never let both sides accept writes. |\n| **Who accepts writes during migration** | **Single writer, moved in a ≤ 2-minute freeze** | Leadership requires literally zero write pause. Then build a write proxy that queues bookings and checks idempotency, which costs about 6–10 more weeks and needs its own rehearsals. |\n| **Migration depth** | **Replatform:** same app build, same database engine, on a managed database (e.g., RDS / Azure SQL MI). Users see no UI change and need no retraining. | Database licensing on the cloud is too expensive or the engine is unsupported. Then change engines as a **separate later project**, never in the same cutover. |\n| **Monolith vs services** | **Keep the monolith.** The only new piece is a thin routing layer (a reverse proxy plus DNS names) in front of it. | One function (e.g., reminders, or portal availability lookups) needs to scale independently. Split it out after Phase 6. |\n| **Sync vs async** | **Async change-data-capture (CDC) replication** for data (AWS DMS / Debezium / GoldenGate, matched to the engine). **Synchronous** writes to whichever side is the single writer. HL7 stays async through the interface engine. | Replication lag p99 > 5 s during the rehearsal window, or CDC can't capture some tables (no primary key, or LOB columns). Then fix the schema or snapshot those tables during the freeze. |\n| **Build vs buy** | **Buy** managed infrastructure: managed database, managed CDC, managed load balancer and firewall, the cloud key service. **Build** only reconciliation, diff tooling and the cutover runbook. | The vendor offers a certified SaaS version. Then this becomes a vendor-led data migration, but gates 1–2 and Phases 1, 4 and 5 still apply. |\n| **Cloud / PHI boundary** | Your existing cloud with a signed BAA, HIPAA-eligible services only, one region inside the jurisdiction, keys you manage, **no public endpoints**. | The portal needs an internet-facing endpoint. Add a WAF-fronted public tier after a pen test (Phase 3). |\n| **Hybrid connectivity** | Dedicated circuit (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute) **plus a site-to-site VPN as failover**. Order it on day 1 because circuits take 6–12 weeks to provision. | The circuit isn't delivered in time. Run Phase 0–1 over a redundant VPN, but **no write cutover over VPN only**. |\n| **(AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune** | N/A | Not an AI system. |\n| **(AI) hosted API vs self-host** | N/A | Not an AI system. |\n\n## 3. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n**The one real request:** a scheduler opens *\"Today's appointments for Dr. X, Clinic Y.\"* The cloud stack serves it from replicated data, and the answer is checked against on-prem's answer for the same request.\n\n**Tiers it crosses:**\n1. Scheduler workstation → hospital DNS, using a new name you control, e.g., `sched.hosp.internal`, that points to a pass-through proxy.\n2. Proxy (NGINX/Envoy, on-prem, initially just forwarding) → hybrid link → private load balancer and WAF in the cloud.\n3. → The app container, the **same build hash as on-prem**, running in a read-only mode, on ECS/AKS.\n4. → Login via SSO federated to hospital AD/Entra, with MFA.\n5. → The managed database replica, fed by CDC from the on-prem database. Phase 0 replicates only the *appointment, slot, provider, location and patient-demographics-reference* tables.\n6. → The real response goes back to 3 pilot schedulers.\n\nAt the same time, the proxy **mirrors** all real read requests of this type to the cloud and compares the cloud's answer with on-prem's. Users always get the on-prem answer, so mirrored traffic has no user impact.\n\n**Deployed, logged, monitored on day 0:**\n- **Deployed:** all of it via Terraform and a CI pipeline (landing zone, network, database, app, proxy config).\n- **Logged:** OpenTelemetry traces cover proxy → app → database. Logs are structured and stripped of PHI, and go to the hospital SIEM. Who-viewed-which-patient access audit logs go to the same audit store as on-prem.\n- **Monitored:** dashboards and alerts for replication lag, cloud vs on-prem diff rate, p95 latency, error rate, and a once-a-minute synthetic check.\n\n**Exit check:** a pilot scheduler's real request gets a correct answer from the cloud in production, with a full trace, a lag metric, and a diff result visible on the dashboard. On-prem is untouched and still the only system accepting bookings.\n\n## 4. Phases (ordered by dependency; within a phase, widest blast radius first)\n\n**Phase 0: Walking skeleton** (above)\n- Unlocks: proof that the hybrid link, identity, CDC, the app build and observability all work end-to-end.\n- Depends on: signed BAA, landing zone, connectivity (VPN acceptable here).\n- Tasks, widest first:\n  1. BAA and the PHI boundary.\n  2. Network and identity federation.\n  3. Pass-through proxy and the DNS name.\n  4. CDC for the core tables.\n  5. Read-only app deploy.\n  6. Request mirroring and diffing.\n  7. Dashboards.\n- Exit: as in §3.\n\n**Phase 1: Data substrate (complete, provable replication)**\n- Unlocks: everything after it. Nothing reads from or writes to the cloud database broadly until this is proven.\n- Depends on: Phase 0 CDC working on the core tables.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Dependency inventory.** Every database, file share, batch job, report, ODBC/thick client, hard-coded IP or hostname, and inbound/outbound interface. Extend CDC to the **full schema** and any other databases the inventory finds.\n  4. **Continuous reconciliation:** per-table row counts every hour, column checksums every night, and an appointment-level comparison of slots booked per provider per day.\n  5. Re-snapshot procedure, tested.\n  6. Repoint the thick clients and reports found in the inventory to DNS names you control. They still resolve to on-prem.\n- Exit: replication lag p99 < 5 s for **14 consecutive days**, zero unexplained reconciliation mismatches for 7 days, and every inventory item has an owner and a migration path.\n\n**Phase 2: Integration layer in shadow**\n- Unlocks: cloud-side HL7/FHIR traffic that can be switched over later.\n- Depends on: Phase 1. The cloud data must be trustworthy before you compare messages generated from it.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Stand up the interface-engine channels in the cloud from version-controlled exports.\n  2. **Inbound ADT/MPI (patient index) feeds copied** to the cloud. FHIR/portal API endpoints, read-only.\n  5. Reminder/SMS vendor connectivity tested with a test-only sender.\n- Exit: zero outbound SIU differences across all event types (S12–S15, S17, S26) for 7 days, and every interface partner has signed off on the connectivity test.\n\n**Phase 3: Read-path cutover (progressive, reversible)**\n- Unlocks: real load on the cloud, and proof that it performs as well as on-prem.\n- Depends on: Phases 1–2. Replicated data is proven, and shadow comparisons are clean.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Lag-gated routing in the proxy: serve reads from the cloud only while replication lag is under 5 s, otherwise fall back to on-prem automatically.\n  2. Canary rollout: 5% → 25% → 100% of read traffic, one department at a time, with the emergency department and surgery scheduling last.\n  3. Patient-portal availability lookups (pen test first if it's public).\n  4. Reports and analytics moved to the cloud replica.\n- Exit: 100% of reads served from the cloud for 14 days, p95 latency at or below the on-prem baseline, no stale-read incidents, and automatic fallback exercised at least once in production.\n\n**Phase 4: Rollback path and rehearsals (must be proven before any write moves)**\n- Unlocks: the write cutover, because now it can be undone without losing data.\n- Depends on: Phase 3 proving the cloud can carry production load.\n- Tasks:\n  1. **Reverse CDC (cloud → on-prem)**, built and validated in a production-like environment.\n  2. Point-in-time restore of the cloud database, actually performed and timed.\n  3. Cutover runbook as scripts, with go/no-go criteria and rollback triggers.\n  4. **3 full dress rehearsals** on a production-sized copy: freeze → drain → verify → switch authority → reverse CDC → **rollback**.\n  5. Game days: kill an availability zone, cut the dedicated circuit, kill the CDC task.\n  6. Clinical-operations sign-off on the ≤ 2-minute freeze, the cutover date, and the downtime-procedure standby.\n- Exit: 3 rehearsals in a row finish within time (freeze ≤ 2 min, rollback ≤ 15 min, zero data loss confirmed by reconciliation), the dedicated circuit is live, and the sign-off is recorded.\n\n**Phase 5: Write-authority cutover**\n- Unlocks: the cloud becomes the system of record.\n- Depends on: Phase 4 exit. A proven rollback path is required.\n- Tasks, in rehearsed order. This order is dictated by the procedure, not by blast radius.\n  1. Change freeze; no other changes allowed, including EHR upgrades or template edits.\n  2. Command center staffed (IT, clinical ops, interface team, vendor).\n  3. The app shows a \"read-only\" banner, and in-flight writes drain.\n  4. Confirm lag = 0 and checksums match.\n  5. Flip the authority flag, so the cloud accepts writes and on-prem becomes read-only.\n  6. Start reverse CDC.\n  7. Switch outbound SIU to the cloud engine and quiesce the on-prem engine.\n  8. Smoke-book a test patient, then release the banner.\n  9. Hypercare for 72 h.\n- Exit: write freeze ≤ 2 min; booking volume within ±10% of the same hour last week; zero interface NACKs (rejected messages) above baseline; reverse-CDC lag < 5 s; no rollback trigger hit in 72 h.\n\n**Phase 6: Stabilize, replace DR, decommission**\n- Unlocks: shutting down on-prem.\n- Depends on: Phase 5 stable for 30 days, **and** a replacement DR proven. On-prem is your DR until then.\n- Tasks:\n  1. Cross-region backup/restore DR with a target RPO ≤ 5 min and RTO ≤ 4 h, tested.\n  2. Run reverse CDC for 30 days, then retire it.\n  3. Archive on-prem data under records retention and legal hold.\n  4. Sanitize media (NIST 800-88) and collect certificates of destruction.\n  5. Remove proxy fallback routes.\n- Exit: a DR restore drill passes, on-prem is powered off with no consumers left (checked against the Phase 1 inventory), and the risk analysis is updated.\n\n## 5.
